276	## Image updates — `internal/imageupdate` (§3.88)
277	
278	Three tables carry an **Update** column (`internal/ui/updatecol`): oci's Images
279	tab, the containers list, and the Remediation tab of a scan result. It shows an
280	arrow when the image's registry holds something newer, and says what:
281	
282	| Kind | When | Cell |
283	|---|---|---|
284	| `NewPatch` | the tag has ≥ 3 version components and a tag differing only by the last, same variant, is higher (`20.11.1-alpine` → `20.11.4-alpine`) | the arrow and the tag |
285	| `NewBuild` | the digest the tag points to now is none of the local image's digests | the arrow alone (`IconArrowDown`) |
286	
287	A newer patch wins over a new build. Every other state says why there is no
288	arrow, in grey — a blank used to stand for all of them, which in the
289	Remediation tab (bases rarely pinned, often not held locally) meant a column
290	that was silent without saying why:
291	
292	| Kind | Cell | When |
293	|---|---|---|
294	| `UpToDate` | the check mark | the local digest is the tag's |
295	| `Pending` | `IconHourglass` | no answer yet |
296	| `Failed` | `IconHelpCircle` | the registry did not answer (logged) |
297	| `LocalBuild` | `IconHammer` | images, containers: no registry digest |
298	| `NotLocal` | `IconCloud` | Remediation: unpinned, and not held by the engine |
299	| `Pinned` | `IconPin` | a digest with no tag: nothing can move |
300	| `None` | blank | the question does not apply (untagged image, unresolved `FROM`) |
301	
302	Every state but a newer patch is one glyph (`updatecol.Cell`): the words cost
303	eleven cells in the widest table there is, and the reason is still spelled out
304	by `G`'s greyed shortcut in the footer and by `?`. `Status.Label` keeps the
305	word, which is what the filter matches. `Evaluate` takes what "no local digest"
306	means to its caller (`LocalBuild` or `NotLocal`). The column's filter only matches an update's label, or `/ca`
307	would find every `local build`. A tag with fewer components (`3.20`,
308	`20`) has no patches of its own — it floats over them, so a new patch moves the
309	tag and the digest says it. That is also the only answer a floating tag
310	(§3.79) ever gets.
311	
312	**The registry's side is cached, the comparison is not.** `imageupdate.Check`
313	keeps, per reference, the tag's digest and the newer patch tag in
314	`~/.devdesk/cache/image-updates.json` — 6 hours for an answer, 30 minutes for a
315	failure (unknown repository, no credentials) so it is not asked on every
316	refresh. `Evaluate` compares with the local digests each time a row is built,
317	so a pull clears the arrow without asking the registry again.
318	
319	**Two requests at most per reference.** The digest is a `HEAD` on the manifest
320	(`oci.ManifestDigest`) accepting an OCI index and a Docker manifest list — a
321	multi-platform tag's digest is the index's, the one `docker pull` records in
322	`RepoDigests`. Docker Hub does not count a `HEAD` against its pull rate limit.
323	The tag list (`oci.ListRegistryTags`) is only read for a tag with a patch
324	component. At most four references are asked at once; credentials are the
325	engine's (`docker.GetStoredCreds`), as for the Remediation tab.
326	
327	**What each view compares with:**
328	
329	- *Images* — the image's own `RepoDigests`, now read by the same `image
330	  inspect` that reads its size (`templates().ImageInspect`). Only a tagged image
331	  **with** a digest is asked about: one built or loaded here has none, and its
332	  name would send the question to a registry that never heard of it.
333	- *Containers* — the digests of the image the container was **created from**
334	  (`docker.ContainerImageDigests`: `container inspect` for the image ID, then
335	  `image inspect`). After a pull the container still runs the old image, so the
336	  arrow stays until it is recreated — which is what it is there to say. The
337	  digests are read again only when the set of containers changes, not on every
338	  two-second refresh.
339	- *Remediation* — the digest the Dockerfile pins, or else the image the engine
340	  holds under that name (`docker.ImageRepoDigests`). A base the engine does not
341	  hold only gets the patch side.
342	
343	`imageupdate.Tracker` is what each view keeps between checks: the facts it has
344	and the references a check is out for, so a reload asks only what is new or
345	stale. Every view reaches the network through a package variable its tests
346	replace.
347	
348	**Updating — `G` on the Images tab.** It pulls what the column points at (the
349	newer patch tag, or the same tag again for a new build) and removes the image
350	it replaces, by ID and never forced. It refuses while any container, running
351	or stopped, was created from that image (`docker.ContainersUsingImage`, `ps -a
352	--filter ancestor=`): removing it would break the container, and keeping it
353	would leave the update half done. The check is made twice — from the engine's
354	container count to grey `G` (Rule 130; docker only, podman reports none), and
355	against the engine just before the pull, since a container can appear in
356	between. A pull that brings the image already held removes nothing
357	(`docker.SameImageID`). It runs as a pull job, so the row spins and `K` stops
358	it; every refusal and failure is a footer line naming why (the containers in
359	use, a failed pull, an old image that could not be removed).
360	
361	**On a narrow terminal**, the containers table drops the two gauges before
362	Update (they are `DropFirst`, §3.71), then the I/O counters, then Update. Both
363	gauges now need 180 columns instead of 160.
364	
365	**Not done**: a digest for a tag the engine holds under another name, and the
366	`podman` side of `RepoDigests` has not been measured against a real `podman
367	system service` — the field exists there under the same name.
368	
369	**From a container to its image — `J`** (§3.89). The containers view sends
370	`ociresources.FocusImageRequestMsg` with the image reference exactly as the
371	engine printed it; the router switches to the OCI view and hands it the
372	request, which waits for the first listing if the view was just built
373	(`deferUntilListed`, the same queue agents use). Matching is the OCI view's
374	(`imageMatches`, `focus.go`): an implicit `latest`, docker's `nginx` against
375	podman's `docker.io/library/nginx`, a registry port that is not a tag, a
376	`repo@sha256:` digest against `RepoDigests`, and a bare ID — what `ps` shows
377	once the tag has moved to a newer image. A search hiding the target is
378	dropped; an image that is no longer listed is a footer `Warn`. There is no
379	`esc` back: `:ct` returns, as from any other view.
380	
381	## The OCI tables and the activity column — `internal/ui/oci_resources` (DEVDESK-146, A-09a; DEVDESK-153, A-09b)
382	
383	The four tables of `:oci` (Images, Networks, Volumes, Registries) and the
384	registry browser's tag table are on the activity column (Rule 125; the router
385	side is in `app-shell.md`).
386	
387	**Periodic refresh and terminal focus (DEVDESK-210).** `refreshInterval` is 10 s
388	(a var, so a test can shorten it). `RefreshTickMsg` used to refresh once and
389	never again; it now re-arms `tickCmd()` on every tick. While `Model.blurred` is
390	set (from `shared.TerminalFocusMsg`) the tick only re-arms and skips
391	`refreshReads()` (images, scan cache, networks, volumes; it never scans, Rule
392	126). On the focus edge (`Resume`) it runs `refreshReads()` once, with no new tick.
393	
394	**Registry browser (DEVDESK-218, A-09a2).** The tag table
395	(`registry_browser.go`, built by `newTagTable`, which `ActivityTables` also uses
396	so the guard sees the real table open or not, as `oci/registry-browser`) takes
397	`datatable.IndicatorColumn` as column 0, an 8th column; Registry, Tag and
398	Updated are 1 to 3 (`tagColumnTag` = 2, `tagColumnUpdated` = 3). `tagRow` holds
399	`Activity components.RowActivity` and `ScanRunning`, stamped by
400	`rebuildTagTable` from `components.DescribeRow` (scan and pull, `ociKinds`,
401	target `jobs.TargetKey(imageName)`) over the snapshot the router pushes through
402	`SetJobs(runs, failures, context)`; the cell at rest is empty. While a scan
403	really runs (not queued) the C/H/M/L cells hold `…` in `DimStyle`; a queued scan
404	or a pull keeps the counts. The blink phase arrives with `SetBlinkPhase` and
405	`WantsBlink` is true for a visible running tag row. Rule 116: Updated drops
406	under 102 columns, L under 84, M under 78, H under 72, C under 66; at 60 only
407	the dot, Registry and Tag remain. The browser has no spinner of its own
408	(DEVDESK-374): a search shows the shared activity dot in the footer
409	(`Searching registries...`), and `WantsBlink` is true while it runs. After the search the
410	footer describes the selected tag (`Status{Detail}`). `tagScanSpinnerIdx` and
411	the local frame are deleted. `DescribeRow` filters by context: a scan of another
412	context no longer shows on a tag (D108).
413	
414	**Cancelling a lot and ignoring late answers (DEVDESK-298, IS-18).** The
415	browser launches requests in lots (one per validation that starts something).
416	`browserGen` is a package-wide `atomic.Uint64`, incremented only from `Update`
417	(`nextBrowserGen`). `beginRequests()` cancels the previous lot (one
418	`CancelFunc`, `cancelRequests`, per lot, not per registry), takes a new
419	generation and resets `pendingSearches`; the `context` is born in `Update`
420	(Rule 110). `MultiRegistryTagsLoadedMsg`, `MultiRegistryTagsMetaMsg` and
421	`ImageSearchResultMsg` carry the `Gen` they were started with, and their
422	handlers return before logging anything when it differs from the open
423	browser's. The counter is global rather than per browser so that a browser
424	closed and reopened, or a new `Model` after a context switch, cannot accept the
425	answer of an older instance. `closeMultiRegistryBrowser` calls
426	`cancelInFlight()`, which also covers closing through `G` (a pull). A validation
427	that starts nothing (empty name, no registry checked) cancels nothing and
428	leaves `gen` alone. The tag lookups go through the `listRegistryTags` variable
429	(`oci.ListRegistryTagsContext`), the seam tests swap to capture the context;
430	there is no deadline on a tag lookup, only `maxTagPages` and the per-request
431	client timeout. `Model.RegistryBrowserGen()` exposes the generation to tests
432	only.
433	
434	**Level 1: image search (DEVDESK-299, IS-01; Open Tags DEVDESK-300, IS-11).**
435	The browser has three states: `browserStateInput` (form), `browserStateImages`
436	(level 1, appended last in the `iota` list) and `browserStateTags` (level 2).
437	
438	*The form's buttons.* `formButtons()` (`browser_form.go`) is the single source
439	of the buttons: the keyboard, the rendering (`renderFormButtons`, one line) and
440	the header (`FormEnter`) all read it. Without a `Searcher` there is one button,
441	`Browse Tags` (action `actionSearch`). With one there are two, `Search`
442	(`actionSearch`) then `Open Tags` (`actionOpenTags`).
443	
444	*Field indices.* Repository is `brFieldRepo` (0); the picker checkboxes are
445	1..n (n = `len(b.rows)`); the buttons follow: `brFieldButton(i)` = `1 + n + i`,
446	and `brFieldLast()` is the last button. `focusedButton()` maps the focus back to
447	a button (false on Repository or a checkbox). `down` stops at `brFieldLast()`.
448	
449	*Validation.* `submit(action)` is common to both actions: an empty name starts
450	nothing; no registry checked sends `RegistryBrowserWarnMsg{"No registry
451	selected"}`, which the `Model` shows as a footer warning (the browser has no
452	footer; this also applies to a name that contains `/`, where the tag flow used
453	to refuse silently). Then `actionOpenTags` always goes to `startTagLookup`
454	(the former code extracted as is, name as typed). `actionSearch` follows the
455	IS-01 rule: a name with no `/` goes to `startImageSearch` when `b.searcher !=
456	nil`, anything else to `startTagLookup`. `enter` on Repository runs
457	`actionSearch`; `enter` on a button runs that button's action; `enter` on a
458	checkbox only advances the focus. The selection applies to both actions.
459	
460	*Header.* `FormEnter()` returns the label and the lit state of the header's
461	single `enter` entry. The label follows the focus: `Search` on Repository and
462	on the Search button (`Browse tags` without a `Searcher`), `Open tags` on the
463	Open Tags button. `enter` is lit on Repository (Rule 130: it submits there) and
464	on a button, and greyed on a checkbox.
465	
466	*Help.* `registryBrowserHelpBody(searchEnabled)` (`view.go`) depends on the
467	mode (Rule 114): without a `Searcher` it names Browse Tags only; with one it
468	describes Search, Open Tags and the shared selection, and the level 1 sentence.
469	
470	**`defaultImageSearcher` is `ByRegistry(HubSearcher{}, CatalogSearcher{})` in
471	production (DEVDESK-301, IS-02; catalog since DEVDESK-306, IS-03), so level 1
472	and Open Tags are active.** `newRegistryBrowser`
473	copies it into `b.searcher`. Tests do not use it: `TestMain`
474	(`ociresources_test.go`) saves it in `productionImageSearcher` and sets
475	`defaultImageSearcher` to `nil` for the whole suite (no test may reach the real
476	Hub), and tests inject a fake with `withImageSearcher`.
477	`TestProductionWiresTheHubSearcher` reads the saved value. `internal/app`
478	injects nothing: its tests avoid level 1 by typing a name with a `/`.

788	## Verified pulls — `internal/imagepull` (§3.82)
789	
790	**Every pull goes through `imagepull.Pull`** — the registry browser's `G`, an
791	update's `G`, an agent's `image_pull_start`. `TestNoPullBypassesTheSignatureCheck`
792	(`internal/ui/oci_resources`) walks `internal/` and fails on any other file
793	naming `docker.PullImageContext`: a second path would be a pull nobody
794	verified. The engine's pull survives in the OCI view only as the seam
795	`pullImageContext`, handed to `imagepull.Deps` by `pullDeps` and called nowhere.
796	
797	The sequence, in `pull.go`:
798	
799	1. `scan.image_verification: off` pulls the tag, as before §3.82.
800	2. `~/.devdesk/trust.yaml` is read on every pull. A file that does not load
801	   **refuses** the pull, naming the error: an unreadable policy is not an empty
802	   one, and falling back to the built-in rules would drop the user's in silence.
803	3. The tag is resolved to a digest (`oci.ManifestDigest`, the index digest
804	   cosign signs). A registry that will not give it is a Failed verdict decided
805	   by the rule that would have applied — a user rule refuses, anything else
806	   pulls the tag and warns.
807	4. `trust.Evaluate` on that digest, with the local image of the same repository
808	   (`RepoDigests`) for continuity. `Block` is an `imagepull.BlockedError`,
809	   whose message is the reason, naming the rule.
810	5. `pull repo@digest`, then `docker.TagImage` back to the name asked for.
811	   Pulling the tag instead would let it move between the check and the pull —
812	   the attack. Measured on Docker and Podman; under Docker's containerd store
813	   `repo@sha256:…` also shows in `RepoTags`, `docker images` lists one row.
814	
815	What the views do with it: a refusal is a footer **Error** naming the rule, and
816	the `:jobs` detail an agent reads is the same sentence; a Warn goes ahead and
817	says why after the pull. The Images tab header shows `Signatures: off`, or
818	`trust.yaml invalid` — read once when the view starts (`checkTrustPolicyCmd`).
819	
820	**The `Sig` column** of the Images tab (`signatures.go`, the shared
821	`internal/ui/sigcol`) is each local image's verdict on the content on disk:
822	`imagepull.LocalDigest` picks the `RepoDigests` entry of the image's own
823	repository, and `imagepull.Check` asks about that digest against the rules
824	alone — continuity would compare the image with itself. An image with no such
825	digest was built or loaded here (a hammer, as in Update). Checked in the
826	background on `ImagesListMsg`, four at a time; `sigAsked` keeps the digest each
827	image was asked about, so an unchanged list asks nothing, a pull that changes
828	the digest asks again, a verdict about a former digest is dropped, and a Failed
829	one is retried after 30 minutes. An image no rule covers is decided without
830	cosign, and one DevDesk pulled comes from the verdict cache. Nothing acts on
831	the column.

833	**`run` never pulls**: `buildLaunchArgs` and `VerifyEntrypoint` pass
834	`--pull=never` (a missing image exits 125, both engines). An image reaches the
835	machine through a verified pull or not at all. DevDesk's own tool images —
836	Trivy, cosign, the netdiag image — are pulled by their `run` and are **not**
837	verified: a declared exception.

1	# Chemin d'un appel réseau (network-map) : brief
2	
3	> Le rapport WSL (`spike-wsl.md`) est livré par une PR distincte.
4	
5	> Brief établi à partir des stories Plane DEVDESK-325 à DEVDESK-335 (S-01 à S-09), de `docs/architecture/network.md`, de `internal/netiface`, `internal/ports` et du stage `route` de `internal/netcheck`, et mis à jour après les spikes du 2026-11-12. Les arbitrages de l'utilisateur sont marqués « Décidé » ; ce qui reste ouvert est marqué **À CONFIRMER** et repris en fin de document.
6	>
7	> Convention de marquage : `Hypothèse:` = supposé non vérifié ; **À CONFIRMER** = décision qui revient à l'utilisateur ; « (story S-xx) » = repris d'une story Plane ; « (code) » = lu dans le dépôt.
8	
9	## Vision
10	
11	Dans la vue Network de DevDesk, un onglet « Path » montre, depuis cette machine, par où passe l'appel vers une cible : source, interface de sortie, passerelle, puis chaque saut, avec l'honnêteté d'un outil qui ne prétend jamais répondre pour une autre machine.
12	
13	## Problème
14	
15	- Quand un appel n'atteint pas sa cible, le dev ne sait pas si le problème est **local, dans son réseau ou plus loin** (S-09).
16	- Quand un VPN capture la route par défaut, les checks actuels rapportent le symptôme (pas de réponse ICMP, pas de connexion TCP) ; le stage `route` de `netcheck` nomme l'interface de sortie et la passerelle, mais **rien n'indique les sauts suivants** (code : `runRoute`, `RouteHop{Interface, Source, Gateway}`).
17	- Sous WSL2, le premier saut est un switch virtuel et non un routeur ; sous Docker Desktop, le chemin interne d'un conteneur n'existe pas sur la machine. Un affichage naïf induit en erreur (S-06, S-07).
18	
19	## Pourquoi pas simplement rétablir l'ancien trace
20	
21	`docs/architecture/network.md` (§3.47) explique que l'ancien trace a été **supprimé, pas réécrit** :
22	
23	- il tournait dans un conteneur `--network host`, donc répondait pour la VM de Docker Desktop et non pour la machine (D57) ;
24	- sa réécriture reposait sur **trois inconnues non mesurées** : lire les ICMP `TIME_EXCEEDED` sans socket brute sur trois plateformes, un TTL par paquet que `pro-bing` n'expose pas, un mode TCP.
25	
26	Ce projet reprend la première inconnue **et seulement sur Linux** (Epic A), comme un spike mesuré avant tout code produit. Il ne contredit pas la décision de §3.47 : le trace s'exécute **dans le processus DevDesk**, sans conteneur et sans binaire externe. Conséquence à documenter à la livraison : `network.md` devra dire que le trace revient, et pourquoi il répond désormais pour la bonne machine.
27	
28	## Utilisateurs
29	
30	- **Mainteneur de DevDesk** (Epic A) : veut savoir si le chemin d'un appel est réalisable avant d'investir (S-01, S-02).
31	- **Dev / DevSecOps utilisateur de DevDesk** (Epic B) : sur Linux natif ou WSL2, parfois derrière un VPN, avec ou sans Docker Engine. Le cas de l'utilisateur actuel est WSL2 + Docker Desktop (S-06, S-02 : « poste Windows de l'utilisateur »).
32	
33	## Solutions existantes
34	
35	| Existant | Ce qu'il couvre | Ce qu'il ne couvre pas |
36	|---|---|---|
37	| Stage `route` de `netcheck` (code) | Interface, adresse source, passerelle pour une adresse, sans privilège, ~2 ms (`go-netroute`) | Les sauts au-delà de la passerelle |
38	| `internal/netiface` (code) | Interfaces de **cette machine** (nom, état, MTU, MAC, adresses v4/v6, compteurs), sans conteneur | Table de routage, ARP, pare-feu (retirés, §3.44) |
39	| `internal/ports` (code) | Sockets locaux et processus | Hors sujet |
40	| Ancien trace (supprimé, §3.47) | Sauts depuis un conteneur `--network host` | Répondait pour la mauvaise machine |
41	| `traceroute`, `mtr`, `tracepath` | Hypothèse: ils existent sur la plupart des postes Linux | **Non étudiés ici.** Le produit exclut de toute façon de lancer un binaire externe (S-03a). |
42	
43	## Périmètre MVP
44	
45	Deux epics, dans cet ordre.
46	
47	**Epic A, « Spike trace natif »** (module Plane du même nom)
48	
49	| Story | Plane | Contenu | Livrable |
50	|---|---|---|---|
51	| S-01 | DEVDESK-325 | Mesurer L1 à L7 sur Linux natif, sur la machine Linux native (Debian 13, noyau 6.12, amd64, utilisateur non-root, accès ssh), cible de référence `1.1.1.1` | `docs/product/network-map/spike-linux.md` + binaire autonome de spike (code jetable sur la branche `spike/nettrace`, jamais fusionnée ; seuls les documents sont fusionnés) |
52	| S-02 | DEVDESK-326 | Mesurer W1 à W5 sur WSL2 NAT et mirrored (mesures faites dans la distro WSL par l'équipe d'agents ; l'utilisateur bascule le mode) | `docs/product/network-map/spike-wsl.md` |
53	
54	**Epic B, « Onglet Path »** (conditionné par le go de l'Epic A)
55	
56	| Story | Plane | Contenu | Dépend de |
57	|---|---|---|---|
58	| S-03a | DEVDESK-327 | Moteur de trace natif `internal/nettrace` | S-01 (go) |
59	| S-03b | DEVDESK-328 | Onglet « Path » : saisie de la cible, lancement, annulation, pré-remplissage depuis une ligne `route` de Diagnostics | S-03a |
60	| S-04 | DEVDESK-329 | Colonne : source, interface + adresse source, passerelle, sauts | S-03a, S-03b |
61	| S-05a | DEVDESK-330 | Conteneur comme source (Docker Engine) | S-04 |
62	| S-05b | DEVDESK-331 | Bridge affiché seulement s'il existe dans les interfaces lues sur cette machine | S-05a |
63	| S-06 | DEVDESK-332 | Ligne « engine » : bridge absent de cette machine (moteur distant, VM, rootless), chemin interne non visible ; Docker Desktop reste non proposé comme source | S-05a, S-05b, S-07 |
64	| S-07 | DEVDESK-333 | Reconnaître WSL2, étiqueter source et premier saut | S-04, résultat de S-02 |
65	| S-08 | DEVDESK-334 | Plateformes ou modes non supportés : onglet grisé, message clair, rien émis | S-03a |
66	| S-09 | DEVDESK-335 | Montrer jusqu'où l'appel va quand il échoue (sans déduire de cause) | S-03a |
67	
68	Contraintes de produit portées par les stories : sans privilège, sans binaire externe, sans conteneur ; sondes en parallèle (8 sauts en moins de 5 s) ; arrêt en 30 s au plus ; annulation sans fuite de sockets ; un saut muet est rapporté muet, jamais comme une panne ; la source est étiquetée « cette machine » ; les lectures d'engine ne démarrent aucun conteneur.
69	
70	## Hors périmètre
71	
72	- Intégration TUI dans le spike (Epic A) ; macOS ; Windows natif ; WSL1 (S-01, S-02).
73	- Mode TCP ; diagnostic automatique de la cause (S-09).
74	- **IPv6** : le spike est IPv4 seul (décidé), donc S-03a l'exclut (« si le spike ne le couvre pas »).
75	- Docker Desktop vu de l'intérieur ; Podman ; réseaux overlay ; Kubernetes ; VM nommées (S-05a, S-05b, S-06).
76	- Un graphe, les switchs (S-04) ; le réseau de Windows vu depuis WSL (S-07).
77	- Support effectif de macOS et Windows : seulement un onglet grisé (S-08).
78	
79	## Plateformes
80	
81	| Plateforme | Statut | Comportement |
82	|---|---|---|
83	| Linux natif | Supporté | Onglet disponible si S-01 réussit |
84	| WSL2, mode NAT | Supporté si W1 réussit en NAT **et** en mirrored, et si le mode est distinguable (W2). **Mesuré : supporté, avec réserves** (`spike-wsl.md`) | Sinon **WSL2 entier est grisé** (S-08, décidé) |
85	| WSL2, mode mirrored | Idem. **Mesuré : supporté, avec réserves** (`spike-wsl.md`) | Idem |
86	| macOS | Grisé | Message plateforme + raison, rien émis (S-08) |
87	| Windows natif | Grisé | Idem |
88	| WSL1 | Grisé | Idem. La détection de WSL1 est vérifiée à l'implémentation de S-08, pas par le spike (décidé) |
89	| Docker Desktop | Non proposé comme source (ctrl+o, DEVDESK-330) | Pas d'étape « VM de l'engine » : la nature de l'engine n'est jamais déduite. La ligne « engine » (S-06) couvre un bridge absent de cette machine (moteur distant, VM, rootless) : chemin interne non visible |
90	
91	## Règle go / no-go
92	
93	1. **L'Epic A précède l'Epic B.** Aucune story de l'Epic B ne démarre avant le verdict de S-01.
94	2. **S-01 échoue => l'Epic B est abandonné** (S-01).
95	3. **Linux OK mais un mode WSL2 KO => on livre, et WSL2 entier est grisé** (S-02, S-08 ; décidé : le mode actif n'étant pas toujours distinguable, on ne grise pas un seul mode). Même règle si W2 conclut que le mode est indistinguable. **Si les deux modes échouent et que Linux natif réussit, on livre pour Linux natif seul, et `spike-wsl.md` l'écrit en toutes lettres.**
96	4. S-01 échoue si l'un des critères L1 à L7 échoue, avec trois exceptions décidées : L3 (plan B : socket bloquant avec délai de lecture) ; L6 (on assouplit le seuil de S-03a, pas de no-go) ; L7 (correction du prototype puis re-mesure, no-go seulement si la fuite est structurelle). L4 et L5 sont bloquants. Le détail critère par critère est dans `feasibility.md`.
97	5. Un spike qui ne conclut pas (mesure impossible, environnement indisponible) n'est ni un go ni un no-go : il est consigné « non évalué » avec la raison, et la décision revient à l'utilisateur.
98	
99	## Hypothèses à valider
100	
101	| # | Hypothèse | Source | Comment la valider |
102	|---|---|---|---|
103	| H1 | UDP + `IP_RECVERR` (stdlib ou `x/sys`) suffit sans privilège | S-01 | L1, L2 |
104	| H2 | Le netpoller Go réveille sur la file d'erreurs ; plan B : socket bloquant avec délai de lecture | S-01 | L3 |
105	| H3 | Passer `x/sys` en dépendance directe est acceptable | S-01 | **Décidé : oui.** Aujourd'hui `golang.org/x/sys v0.49.0 // indirect` dans `go.mod` (code) ; le passage se fait avec le code produit de S-03a, avec Rule 303 (tidy/verify) et documentation |
106	| H4 | Le comportement de S-01 se retrouve en WSL2 NAT ; en mirrored les Time Exceeded peuvent ne jamais arriver | S-02 | W1. **Levée** : les Time Exceeded arrivent en mirrored comme en NAT (`spike-wsl.md`) |
107	| H5 | S-02 donne une détection fiable du mode WSL2 | S-07 | W2. **Confirmée** : `wslinfo --networking-mode` rend `nat` ou `mirrored` (`spike-wsl.md`, WSL 2.7.13.0 ; non testé sur un WSL plus ancien) |
108	| H6 | Le stage `route` fournit interface et passerelle | S-04 | Déjà confirmé par la lecture du code (`Env.Route` rend `RouteHop`) ; reste à choisir comment le réutiliser depuis l'onglet |
109	| H7 | L'onglet se branche comme les autres tabs de `netdiag` ; l'affichage passe par un `datatable` (sinon S devient M) | S-03b, S-04 | Revue de `internal/ui/netdiag` à l'architecte |
110	| H8 | Les infos d'un conteneur (réseau, IP, passerelle) se lisent par l'inspection d'engine existante | S-05a | Non vérifié ici. `internal/docker/networks.go` expose `InspectNetwork` ; l'inspection de conteneur reste à confirmer |
111	| H9 | `internal/netiface` suffit pour tester l'existence du bridge | S-05b | W5 (côté WSL) ; test unitaire avec fausses interfaces |
112	| H10 | L'absence du bridge sur la machine est le bon signal d'un engine distant ou en VM | S-06 | W4, W5 |
113	| H11 | WSL1 se détecte de façon fiable | S-08 | Vérifiée à l'implémentation de S-08, aucun constat dans S-02 (décidé) |
114	| H12 | Un saut muet est le plus souvent un filtrage ICMP | S-09 | Information seulement : l'UI n'en déduit aucune cause |
115	
116	## Libellés d'interface
117	
118	Les stories décrivent les textes en français. La Rule 129 impose l'anglais US dans l'UI. Proposition de formulation (à valider à l'implémentation, pas encore une décision) :
119	
120	| Story | Libellé proposé |
121	|---|---|
122	| « cette machine » (S-04) | `this machine` |
123	| « WSL2 (VM), pas l'hôte Windows » (S-07) | **Décidé (DEVDESK-333)** : ligne source `WSL2 (VM), not the Windows host · NAT mode`, `· mirrored mode` ou `· mode unknown` |

# Chemin d'un appel réseau (network-map) : brief

> Le rapport WSL (`spike-wsl.md`) est livré par une PR distincte.

> Brief établi à partir des stories Plane DEVDESK-325 à DEVDESK-335 (S-01 à S-09), de `docs/architecture/network.md`, de `internal/netiface`, `internal/ports` et du stage `route` de `internal/netcheck`, et mis à jour après les spikes du 2026-11-12. Les arbitrages de l'utilisateur sont marqués « Décidé » ; ce qui reste ouvert est marqué **À CONFIRMER** et repris en fin de document.
>
> Convention de marquage : `Hypothèse:` = supposé non vérifié ; **À CONFIRMER** = décision qui revient à l'utilisateur ; « (story S-xx) » = repris d'une story Plane ; « (code) » = lu dans le dépôt.

## Vision

Dans la vue Network de DevDesk, un onglet « Path » montre, depuis cette machine, par où passe l'appel vers une cible : source, interface de sortie, passerelle, puis chaque saut, avec l'honnêteté d'un outil qui ne prétend jamais répondre pour une autre machine.

## Problème

- Quand un appel n'atteint pas sa cible, le dev ne sait pas si le problème est **local, dans son réseau ou plus loin** (S-09).
- Quand un VPN capture la route par défaut, les checks actuels rapportent le symptôme (pas de réponse ICMP, pas de connexion TCP) ; le stage `route` de `netcheck` nomme l'interface de sortie et la passerelle, mais **rien n'indique les sauts suivants** (code : `runRoute`, `RouteHop{Interface, Source, Gateway}`).
- Sous WSL2, le premier saut est un switch virtuel et non un routeur ; sous Docker Desktop, le chemin interne d'un conteneur n'existe pas sur la machine. Un affichage naïf induit en erreur (S-06, S-07).

## Pourquoi pas simplement rétablir l'ancien trace

`docs/architecture/network.md` (§3.47) explique que l'ancien trace a été **supprimé, pas réécrit** :

- il tournait dans un conteneur `--network host`, donc répondait pour la VM de Docker Desktop et non pour la machine (D57) ;
- sa réécriture reposait sur **trois inconnues non mesurées** : lire les ICMP `TIME_EXCEEDED` sans socket brute sur trois plateformes, un TTL par paquet que `pro-bing` n'expose pas, un mode TCP.

Ce projet reprend la première inconnue **et seulement sur Linux** (Epic A), comme un spike mesuré avant tout code produit. Il ne contredit pas la décision de §3.47 : le trace s'exécute **dans le processus DevDesk**, sans conteneur et sans binaire externe. Conséquence à documenter à la livraison : `network.md` devra dire que le trace revient, et pourquoi il répond désormais pour la bonne machine.

## Utilisateurs

- **Mainteneur de DevDesk** (Epic A) : veut savoir si le chemin d'un appel est réalisable avant d'investir (S-01, S-02).
- **Dev / DevSecOps utilisateur de DevDesk** (Epic B) : sur Linux natif ou WSL2, parfois derrière un VPN, avec ou sans Docker Engine. Le cas de l'utilisateur actuel est WSL2 + Docker Desktop (S-06, S-02 : « poste Windows de l'utilisateur »).

## Solutions existantes

| Existant | Ce qu'il couvre | Ce qu'il ne couvre pas |
|---|---|---|
| Stage `route` de `netcheck` (code) | Interface, adresse source, passerelle pour une adresse, sans privilège, ~2 ms (`go-netroute`) | Les sauts au-delà de la passerelle |
| `internal/netiface` (code) | Interfaces de **cette machine** (nom, état, MTU, MAC, adresses v4/v6, compteurs), sans conteneur | Table de routage, ARP, pare-feu (retirés, §3.44) |
| `internal/ports` (code) | Sockets locaux et processus | Hors sujet |
| Ancien trace (supprimé, §3.47) | Sauts depuis un conteneur `--network host` | Répondait pour la mauvaise machine |
| `traceroute`, `mtr`, `tracepath` | Hypothèse: ils existent sur la plupart des postes Linux | **Non étudiés ici.** Le produit exclut de toute façon de lancer un binaire externe (S-03a). |

## Périmètre MVP

Deux epics, dans cet ordre.

**Epic A, « Spike trace natif »** (module Plane du même nom)

| Story | Plane | Contenu | Livrable |
|---|---|---|---|
| S-01 | DEVDESK-325 | Mesurer L1 à L7 sur Linux natif, sur la machine Linux native (Debian 13, noyau 6.12, amd64, utilisateur non-root, accès ssh), cible de référence `1.1.1.1` | `docs/product/network-map/spike-linux.md` + binaire autonome de spike (code jetable sur la branche `spike/nettrace`, jamais fusionnée ; seuls les documents sont fusionnés) |
| S-02 | DEVDESK-326 | Mesurer W1 à W5 sur WSL2 NAT et mirrored (mesures faites dans la distro WSL par l'équipe d'agents ; l'utilisateur bascule le mode) | `docs/product/network-map/spike-wsl.md` |

**Epic B, « Onglet Path »** (conditionné par le go de l'Epic A)

| Story | Plane | Contenu | Dépend de |
|---|---|---|---|
| S-03a | DEVDESK-327 | Moteur de trace natif `internal/nettrace` | S-01 (go) |
| S-03b | DEVDESK-328 | Onglet « Path » : saisie de la cible, lancement, annulation, pré-remplissage depuis une ligne `route` de Diagnostics | S-03a |
| S-04 | DEVDESK-329 | Colonne : source, interface + adresse source, passerelle, sauts | S-03a, S-03b |
| S-05a | DEVDESK-330 | Conteneur comme source (Docker Engine) | S-04 |
| S-05b | DEVDESK-331 | Bridge affiché seulement s'il existe dans les interfaces lues sur cette machine | S-05a |
| S-06 | DEVDESK-332 | Ligne « engine » : bridge absent de cette machine (moteur distant, VM, rootless), chemin interne non visible ; Docker Desktop reste non proposé comme source | S-05a, S-05b, S-07 |
| S-07 | DEVDESK-333 | Reconnaître WSL2, étiqueter source et premier saut | S-04, résultat de S-02 |
| S-08 | DEVDESK-334 | Plateformes ou modes non supportés : onglet grisé, message clair, rien émis | S-03a |
| S-09 | DEVDESK-335 | Montrer jusqu'où l'appel va quand il échoue (sans déduire de cause) | S-03a |

Contraintes de produit portées par les stories : sans privilège, sans binaire externe, sans conteneur ; sondes en parallèle (8 sauts en moins de 5 s) ; arrêt en 30 s au plus ; annulation sans fuite de sockets ; un saut muet est rapporté muet, jamais comme une panne ; la source est étiquetée « cette machine » ; les lectures d'engine ne démarrent aucun conteneur.

## Hors périmètre

- Intégration TUI dans le spike (Epic A) ; macOS ; Windows natif ; WSL1 (S-01, S-02).
- Mode TCP ; diagnostic automatique de la cause (S-09).
- **IPv6** : le spike est IPv4 seul (décidé), donc S-03a l'exclut (« si le spike ne le couvre pas »).
- Docker Desktop vu de l'intérieur ; Podman ; réseaux overlay ; Kubernetes ; VM nommées (S-05a, S-05b, S-06).
- Un graphe, les switchs (S-04) ; le réseau de Windows vu depuis WSL (S-07).
- Support effectif de macOS et Windows : seulement un onglet grisé (S-08).

## Plateformes

| Plateforme | Statut | Comportement |
|---|---|---|
| Linux natif | Supporté | Onglet disponible si S-01 réussit |
| WSL2, mode NAT | Supporté si W1 réussit en NAT **et** en mirrored, et si le mode est distinguable (W2). **Mesuré : supporté, avec réserves** (`spike-wsl.md`) | Sinon **WSL2 entier est grisé** (S-08, décidé) |
| WSL2, mode mirrored | Idem. **Mesuré : supporté, avec réserves** (`spike-wsl.md`) | Idem |
| macOS | Grisé | Message plateforme + raison, rien émis (S-08) |
| Windows natif | Grisé | Idem |
| WSL1 | Grisé | Idem. La détection de WSL1 est vérifiée à l'implémentation de S-08, pas par le spike (décidé) |
| Docker Desktop | Non proposé comme source (ctrl+o, DEVDESK-330) | Pas d'étape « VM de l'engine » : la nature de l'engine n'est jamais déduite. La ligne « engine » (S-06) couvre un bridge absent de cette machine (moteur distant, VM, rootless) : chemin interne non visible |

## Règle go / no-go

1. **L'Epic A précède l'Epic B.** Aucune story de l'Epic B ne démarre avant le verdict de S-01.
2. **S-01 échoue => l'Epic B est abandonné** (S-01).
3. **Linux OK mais un mode WSL2 KO => on livre, et WSL2 entier est grisé** (S-02, S-08 ; décidé : le mode actif n'étant pas toujours distinguable, on ne grise pas un seul mode). Même règle si W2 conclut que le mode est indistinguable. **Si les deux modes échouent et que Linux natif réussit, on livre pour Linux natif seul, et `spike-wsl.md` l'écrit en toutes lettres.**
4. S-01 échoue si l'un des critères L1 à L7 échoue, avec trois exceptions décidées : L3 (plan B : socket bloquant avec délai de lecture) ; L6 (on assouplit le seuil de S-03a, pas de no-go) ; L7 (correction du prototype puis re-mesure, no-go seulement si la fuite est structurelle). L4 et L5 sont bloquants. Le détail critère par critère est dans `feasibility.md`.
5. Un spike qui ne conclut pas (mesure impossible, environnement indisponible) n'est ni un go ni un no-go : il est consigné « non évalué » avec la raison, et la décision revient à l'utilisateur.

## Hypothèses à valider

| # | Hypothèse | Source | Comment la valider |
|---|---|---|---|
| H1 | UDP + `IP_RECVERR` (stdlib ou `x/sys`) suffit sans privilège | S-01 | L1, L2 |
| H2 | Le netpoller Go réveille sur la file d'erreurs ; plan B : socket bloquant avec délai de lecture | S-01 | L3 |
| H3 | Passer `x/sys` en dépendance directe est acceptable | S-01 | **Décidé : oui.** Aujourd'hui `golang.org/x/sys v0.49.0 // indirect` dans `go.mod` (code) ; le passage se fait avec le code produit de S-03a, avec Rule 303 (tidy/verify) et documentation |
| H4 | Le comportement de S-01 se retrouve en WSL2 NAT ; en mirrored les Time Exceeded peuvent ne jamais arriver | S-02 | W1. **Levée** : les Time Exceeded arrivent en mirrored comme en NAT (`spike-wsl.md`) |
| H5 | S-02 donne une détection fiable du mode WSL2 | S-07 | W2. **Confirmée** : `wslinfo --networking-mode` rend `nat` ou `mirrored` (`spike-wsl.md`, WSL 2.7.13.0 ; non testé sur un WSL plus ancien) |
| H6 | Le stage `route` fournit interface et passerelle | S-04 | Déjà confirmé par la lecture du code (`Env.Route` rend `RouteHop`) ; reste à choisir comment le réutiliser depuis l'onglet |
| H7 | L'onglet se branche comme les autres tabs de `netdiag` ; l'affichage passe par un `datatable` (sinon S devient M) | S-03b, S-04 | Revue de `internal/ui/netdiag` à l'architecte |
| H8 | Les infos d'un conteneur (réseau, IP, passerelle) se lisent par l'inspection d'engine existante | S-05a | Non vérifié ici. `internal/docker/networks.go` expose `InspectNetwork` ; l'inspection de conteneur reste à confirmer |
| H9 | `internal/netiface` suffit pour tester l'existence du bridge | S-05b | W5 (côté WSL) ; test unitaire avec fausses interfaces |
| H10 | L'absence du bridge sur la machine est le bon signal d'un engine distant ou en VM | S-06 | W4, W5 |
| H11 | WSL1 se détecte de façon fiable | S-08 | Vérifiée à l'implémentation de S-08, aucun constat dans S-02 (décidé) |
| H12 | Un saut muet est le plus souvent un filtrage ICMP | S-09 | Information seulement : l'UI n'en déduit aucune cause |

| Story | Libellé proposé |
|---|---|
| « cette machine » (S-04) | `this machine` |
| « WSL2 (VM), pas l'hôte Windows » (S-07) | **Décidé (DEVDESK-333)** : ligne source `WSL2 (VM), not the Windows host · NAT mode`, `· mirrored mode` ou `· mode unknown` |

| ligne « engine », bridge absent de cette machine (S-06) | `internal path not visible (location unknown)` ; en cas de doute : `undetermined (bridge not verified)` |
| « VM » (S-06) | `Engine VM`, affiché seulement si l'engine se déclare VM (non fait) |
| « pas de réponse au-delà » (S-09) | `no response beyond` |
| muet (S-03a, S-09) | `silent` (le mot « muet » ne désigne pas une panne) |
| « indéterminé » (S-05a) | `undetermined` |

## Risques

19	## Pourquoi pas simplement rétablir l'ancien trace
20	
21	`docs/architecture/network.md` (§3.47) explique que l'ancien trace a été **supprimé, pas réécrit** :
22	
23	- il tournait dans un conteneur `--network host`, donc répondait pour la VM de Docker Desktop et non pour la machine (D57) ;
24	- sa réécriture reposait sur **trois inconnues non mesurées** : lire les ICMP `TIME_EXCEEDED` sans socket brute sur trois plateformes, un TTL par paquet que `pro-bing` n'expose pas, un mode TCP.
25	
26	Ce projet reprend la première inconnue **et seulement sur Linux** (Epic A), comme un spike mesuré avant tout code produit. Il ne contredit pas la décision de §3.47 : le trace s'exécute **dans le processus DevDesk**, sans conteneur et sans binaire externe. Conséquence à documenter à la livraison : `network.md` devra dire que le trace revient, et pourquoi il répond désormais pour la bonne machine.

Même règle si W2 conclut que le mode est indistinguable. **Si les deux modes échouent et que Linux natif réussit, on livre pour Linux natif seul, et `spike-wsl.md` l'écrit en toutes lettres.**

S-01 échoue si l'un des critères L1 à L7 échoue, avec trois exceptions décidées : L3 (plan B : socket bloquant avec délai de lecture) ; L6 (on assouplit le seuil de S-03a, pas de no-go) ; L7 (correction du prototype puis re-mesure, no-go seulement si la fuite est structurelle). ## Network Diagnostics View

`internal/ui/netdiag/` — five tabs:
- **Diagnostics tab** (`model.go`): target, port and resolver, then
  `internal/netcheck`'s pipeline — resolve, route, reach, connect, TLS, HTTP —
  chained one stage per message so the footer can name the question being asked.
  The seven tool checkboxes are gone (§3.33): the checks follow from the target
  and from what has already failed.
- **Ports tab** (`ports_model.go`): the machine's own socket table, re-read
  every `ports_refresh_interval`, filtered by protocol, state and text. `K`
  terminates a process, after a confirmation. It runs **no container** — see
  `internal/ports` below. Column 0 is the activity column (DEVDESK-150, below).
- **Interfaces tab** (`interfaces_model.go`): this machine's network interfaces
  — name, state, MTU, MAC, RX/TX error counters, addresses — in a `datatable`.
  It runs **no container**; see `internal/netiface` below. It was the Topology
  tab, and §3.44 is why three of its four sections are gone rather than
  translated.
- **Forward tab** (`forward_model.go`, `forward_form.go`): the port
  redirections, `N` to open one, `space` to pause or resume it and `K` to delete
  it. It holds **no listener** — see `internal/forward` below.
- **Path tab** (`path_model.go`, `path_view.go`, `path_run.go`,
  `path_target.go`, `path_from_route.go`, `path_steps.go`; DEVDESK-328,
  DEVDESK-329): the hop-by-hop path to
  a target, from `internal/nettrace` (below). It is the fifth and last tab
  (`tabPath = 4`, `tabCount = 5`). It runs **no container**; since DEVDESK-330 it
  can name a running Docker Engine container as the source of the column (below),
  but the probes still leave from this machine. Three states:
  `pathEditing` (the target field has the keyboard), `pathRunning` (field
  blurred, hops arriving) and `pathDone` (hops kept on screen). The **body is
  always the hop table** (`PathModel.view()` returns `table.View()`, Rule 139),
  in every state: columns Hop, Step, Address, RTT, with a silent hop dim and
  never red. **The column starts on this machine** (DEVDESK-329): three local
  rows, then the hops. `source` reads `this machine`; `interface` reads
  `<name> (<source address>)`; `gateway` reads the gateway address. The local
  rows have an empty Hop and RTT (they asked nobody; `-` means "no answer") and
  the default text colour. `pathSteps` (`path_steps.go`) is the only place that
  orders the rows; the table item is a `pathStep` (kind source, interface,
  gateway or hop; DEVDESK-330 adds container, network and trace, below).

  error leaves 0 rows. The **target field is not in the body**: it sits in the footer's
  bar slot, framed by `components.BarFrame` (`Target › ` + the field,

  and done. The tab keeps its own `FooterMessage`, returned by `activeFooter`,
  so `WantsBlink()` follows a running trace. `Model.Running()` is true while a
  trace runs, so the router does not rebuild the view mid-trace.

  cancels a running trace, and returns a finished one to editing with the
  value kept; `tab` switches tab; `up`, `down`, `pgup`, `pgdown`, `home` and
  `end` move in the table in every state. While editing, `esc`, `tab` and
  `shift+tab` do nothing in the field. A paste reaches the field only while
  editing (Rule 111). A changed field value clears the persistent error.
  `ctrl+o` opens the "Trace from" selector in `pathEditing` and `pathDone`; while
  a trace runs it warns `A path trace is running — esc cancels it`, and where the
  trace is unsupported it warns with the platform reason (`sourceChoosable`, the
  one answer the header and the handler both read). While the selector is open it
  holds every key: `up`, `down`, `pgup`, `pgdown`, `home` and `end` move, `enter`

  included (`netdiag.Model.Update` hands the key to the Path model before the tab
  switch). A paste is dropped. `PathModel.InEditMode()` is true while it is open,
  so `q` and `:` reach the view and do not quit or open the palette.

**Ports tab, terminal blurred (DEVDESK-210).** `PortsModel.unfocused` is set by
`shared.TerminalFocusMsg`, which `netdiag.Model.Update` forwards to the ports
poll whichever tab shows (the tick runs on every tab). The tick chain is kept:
`handleTick` re-arms `portsTickCmd` and skips `fetchPortsCmd` while `unfocused`.

not doubled. `unfocused` is separate from `paused`, the user's own pause (shown

  |---|---|
  | all | 103 |

1551	## The socket table — `internal/ports`
1552	
1553	The machine's TCP and UDP sockets, and the process holding each, read **in this
1554	process**. `List(ctx, resolve)` and `Kill(pid)` are the whole interface.
1555	
1556	**It exists because the old one answered for the wrong machine** (D55). The
1557	Ports tab ran `ss -tupan` inside
1558	`docker run --rm --net=host --pid=host --privileged`, and on Docker Desktop
1559	`--net=host` is the namespace of the Linux VM: the tab listed the VM's NFS
1560	daemons with two-digit PIDs while not one of the host's 38 listening sockets
1561	appeared, and `K` sent SIGKILL to a process of the VM under the impression it was
1562	freeing a port on the machine. The sentence explaining this has sat at the top of
1563	`docker.runDiagHost` since §3.33 rapatriated DNS, ICMP, TCP, TLS and HTTP for
1564	exactly the same reason; `RunSS` and `KillProcess` were the two nobody pulled it
1565	for. **Under Linux the defect did not exist**, which is why it went unnoticed:
1566	the tab was right on the platform it was written on.
1567	
1568	No new dependency: `gopsutil/v4/net` was already imported by
1569	`internal/metrics/host.go`. Windows reads iphlpapi, Linux `/proc`, macOS and the
1570	BSDs `lsof` — the last is a subprocess, but one the system supplies, and it
1571	replaces a privileged container.
1572

## The socket table — `internal/ports`

The machine's TCP and UDP sockets, and the process holding each, read **in this
process**. `List(ctx, resolve)` and `Kill(pid)` are the whole interface.

**It exists because the old one answered for the wrong machine** (D55). The
Ports tab ran `ss -tupan` inside
`docker run --rm --net=host --pid=host --privileged`, and on Docker Desktop
`--net=host` is the namespace of the Linux VM: the tab listed the VM's NFS
daemons with two-digit PIDs while not one of the host's 38 listening sockets
appeared, and `K` sent SIGKILL to a process of the VM under the impression it was
freeing a port on the machine. The sentence explaining this has sat at the top of
`docker.runDiagHost` since §3.33 rapatriated DNS, ICMP, TCP, TLS and HTTP for
exactly the same reason; `RunSS` and `KillProcess` were the two nobody pulled it
for. **Under Linux the defect did not exist**, which is why it went unnoticed:
the tab was right on the platform it was written on.

No new dependency: `gopsutil/v4/net` was already imported by
`internal/metrics/host.go`. Windows reads iphlpapi, Linux `/proc`, macOS and the
BSDs `lsof` — the last is a subprocess, but one the system supplies, and it
replaces a privileged container.

  obvious `process.NewProcess(pid).Name()` goes through `OpenProcess` on

  every service on the box. `Processes()` reads a Toolhelp32 snapshot instead
  and named **294 of 294** in 11 ms, elevated or not. The bulk call is not an
  optimisation over the per-PID one — it is the difference between a column that
  is filled in and one that is not.

  socket, and `K` keys on that field: left as `"0"` the row would look killable,
  and process 0 is a whole process group on Unix. `Kill` refuses it a second
  time, on the model of §3.23's double guard. The name is a *separate* question:
  a row may know which process holds the socket and not what it is called, and
  it must stay killable — that is the row the user is acting on.

  datagram socket is `NONE` on Linux and nothing at all on Windows, so the same

  column is ten cells wide, so the long spelling renders as `ESTABLISHE`.
- **`n` resolves the host half only.** `ss` without `-n` also turned 22 into
  `ssh`; Go resolves a name to a port and not the other way round, so honouring
  that would mean shipping a copy of `/etc/services` and calling the result the
  system's answer. Saying less beats saying something the system did not.

The reverse-DNS cache is **package-level**, because the lookups run inside a
`Cmd` and a `Cmd` may not touch the model (Rule 110). It caches the failures
too: a machine talking to hosts with no PTR record would otherwise re-ask for
every one of them on every two-second tick — the storm the cache exists to
prevent, arriving through the failures instead of the successes. Wildcard,
loopback and unspecified addresses are never asked at all.

**`Kill` signals with the rights DevDesk has**, which is the visible change:
another user's process, or a service, now comes back refused by the operating
system instead of succeeding against the wrong machine.

**So the refusal has to be legible, and `K` has to say when it cannot even
try** (§3.49). Two different questions, and only one of them is answerable
before the keypress:

- **No PID, no key.** A socket the system declines to attribute carries an empty
  `PID`, and `K` is greyed on that row (Rule 130) — it used to be advertised
  everywhere and warn only once pressed.
- **Whether the OS will accept the signal is the attempt's answer**, never the
  header's, so a row with a PID stays lit even when the kill is certain to be
  refused. `killFailureMessage` classifies the failure with `errors.Is` through
  the `%w` wrapping `Kill` applies: `os.ErrPermission` reads *Refused by the
  system*, `os.ErrProcessDone` reads *no longer running*, anything else keeps
  the generic line. `Failed to kill PID N` made those the same sentence.

The platform error never reaches the screen — measured, PID 4 on this machine
answers `OpenProcess: Accès refusé.`, in the machine's own language, which is
the route stage's rule (§3.44). Also measured, and written down rather than
discovered: **the "already gone" branch does not fire on Windows**, where a
nonexistent PID fails `OpenProcess` with `ERROR_INVALID_PARAMETER` and maps to
neither sentinel. Mapping that code would be a guess, and the row disappears on
the next two-second refresh anyway.

§3.44 the interfaces, and §3.47 removed the route trace — the last one. That is

**The route trace was deleted rather than rewritten** (it came back in the

- it answered for the **wrong machine** — `--network host` traced from the Docker

## The port forwarder — `internal/forward`

A local TCP port redirected to a `host:port`, **in this process** and with no

839	## Network Diagnostics View
840	
841	`internal/ui/netdiag/` — five tabs:
842	- **Diagnostics tab** (`model.go`): target, port and resolver, then
843	  `internal/netcheck`'s pipeline — resolve, route, reach, connect, TLS, HTTP —
844	  chained one stage per message so the footer can name the question being asked.
845	  The seven tool checkboxes are gone (§3.33): the checks follow from the target
846	  and from what has already failed.
847	- **Ports tab** (`ports_model.go`): the machine's own socket table, re-read
848	  every `ports_refresh_interval`, filtered by protocol, state and text. `K`
849	  terminates a process, after a confirmation. It runs **no container** — see
850	  `internal/ports` below. Column 0 is the activity column (DEVDESK-150, below).
851	- **Interfaces tab** (`interfaces_model.go`): this machine's network interfaces
852	  — name, state, MTU, MAC, RX/TX error counters, addresses — in a `datatable`.
853	  It runs **no container**; see `internal/netiface` below. It was the Topology
854	  tab, and §3.44 is why three of its four sections are gone rather than
855	  translated.
856	- **Forward tab** (`forward_model.go`, `forward_form.go`): the port
857	  redirections, `N` to open one, `space` to pause or resume it and `K` to delete
858	  it. It holds **no listener** — see `internal/forward` below.
859	- **Path tab** (`path_model.go`, `path_view.go`, `path_run.go`,
860	  `path_target.go`, `path_from_route.go`, `path_steps.go`; DEVDESK-328,
861	  DEVDESK-329): the hop-by-hop path to
862	  a target, from `internal/nettrace` (below). It is the fifth and last tab
863	  (`tabPath = 4`, `tabCount = 5`). It runs **no container**; since DEVDESK-330 it
864	  can name a running Docker Engine container as the source of the column (below),
865	  but the probes still leave from this machine. Three states:
866	  `pathEditing` (the target field has the keyboard), `pathRunning` (field
867	  blurred, hops arriving) and `pathDone` (hops kept on screen). The **body is
868	  always the hop table** (`PathModel.view()` returns `table.View()`, Rule 139),
869	  in every state: columns Hop, Step, Address, RTT, with a silent hop dim and
870	  never red. **The column starts on this machine** (DEVDESK-329): three local
871	  rows, then the hops. `source` reads `this machine`; `interface` reads
872	  `<name> (<source address>)`; `gateway` reads the gateway address. The local
873	  rows have an empty Hop and RTT (they asked nobody; `-` means "no answer") and
874	  the default text colour. `pathSteps` (`path_steps.go`) is the only place that
875	  orders the rows; the table item is a `pathStep` (kind source, interface,
876	  gateway or hop; DEVDESK-330 adds container, network and trace, below).
877	  Nothing is shown before the route is known, so a resolution
878	  error leaves 0 rows. The **target field is not in the body**: it sits in the footer's
879	  bar slot, framed by `components.BarFrame` (`Target › ` + the field,
880	  placeholder `hostname or IPv4 address[:port]`). That slot is shown on this
881	  tab in every state, so `GetFooterHeight()` is 5 (bar 2, tab row 1, blank
882	  line 1, info line 1) and the layout does not move between editing, running
883	  and done. The tab keeps its own `FooterMessage`, returned by `activeFooter`,
884	  so `WantsBlink()` follows a running trace. `Model.Running()` is true while a
885	  trace runs, so the router does not rebuild the view mid-trace.
886	
887	  Keys: `enter` launches (while editing) or traces again (when done); `esc`
888	  cancels a running trace, and returns a finished one to editing with the
889	  value kept; `tab` switches tab; `up`, `down`, `pgup`, `pgdown`, `home` and
890	  `end` move in the table in every state. While editing, `esc`, `tab` and

892	  editing (Rule 111). A changed field value clears the persistent error.

981	nothing to break down — TCP, TLS). `stage_http.go`'s `httpPhases` derives
982	**Wait** and **Content** rather than charting TTFB directly, because TTFB is
983	measured from the start of the request and already contains DNS+connect+TLS —
984	charting it as a fifth independent share would double-count that overlap.
985	`internal/ui/netdiag/view.go`'s `phaseLines` renders one proportional bar per
986	phase, reusing the load-gauge machinery (`theme.GaugeFill`, `GaugeTrack`,
987	`GaugeFillWidth`, `GaugeTrackStyle`) with a new neutral fill colour, `theme.TimingFillStyle` —
988	a phase taking most of the time is a fact to read, not a severity to spot.
989	
990	**Opened prefilled, from elsewhere (§3.66).** `netdiag.NewWithTarget` builds a
991	view with the form filled in but not yet run; `netdiag.OpenRequestMsg` is
992	what a producer elsewhere sends to ask the router for one (mirroring
993	`uiviewer.OpenRequestMsg`), and `netdiag.BackToOriginMsg` is how `esc` gets
994	back out, via `Model.OriginView` — empty when netdiag was opened directly
995	from the command line, in which case `esc` behaves exactly as it always has.
996	`status`'s `H` (`keymap.Diagnose`, `internal/ui/status/diagnostics.go`) is
997	the first producer: it resolves the selected monitor's target and
998	auto-runs the pipeline when the port is certain (http/https/ssl), or lands on
999	the prefilled form when it is a guess (icmp/dns).
1000	
1001	`H` has a **second producer, inside netdiag** (DEVDESK-328,
1002	`path_from_route.go`): on the Diagnostics results, with the **Local route** row
1003	(`netcheck.CheckRoute`) selected, it switches to the Path tab and fills the
1004	target field with the results' host. It **prefills and never launches**:
1005	nothing is resolved or sent until `enter` on the Path tab. Only the host is
1006	carried over, not the port (the route check does not depend on one).
1007	`pathFromRoute()` is the one availability read by the header (the entry
1008	`H Trace the path` is greyed off the route row, Rule 130) and by the handler,
1009	which otherwise warns `Select the Local route row to trace its path`. If a
1010	trace is already running, `H` switches to the Path tab, leaves the field
1011	alone and warns `A path trace is already running — esc cancels it` on the Path
1012	footer. `PathModel.prefill` puts the tab back in editing with the hops, the
1013	outcome and the error cleared.
1014	
1015	**What is configurable, and what is not.** `internal/netcheck` held its timeouts
1016	as constants with a comment saying they would become settings when somebody
1017	asked; `network:` is what they became.
1018	
1019	| Setting | Replaces |
1020	|---|---|
1021	| `check_timeout` | five per-stage constants — 5 s for DNS and the dial, 8 s for TLS and HTTP, 4 s for the ping |
1022	| `ping_count` | `pingCount` |
1023	| `cert_expiry_warn_days` | `expiryWarnWindow` |
1024	| `ports_refresh_interval` | the 2 s tick |
1025	
1026	**One timeout replaces five**, and the default is the old *maximum* so nothing
1027	that answers today starts failing. The 5 / 5 / 8 / 8 / 4 split was never argued
1028	anywhere — five rows for one idea, and each of the five a separate guess. The
1029	cost is stated rather than discovered: an unreachable host now spends 8 s on DNS
1030	instead of 5, which the staged progress line makes legible rather than a hang.
1031	
1032	`traceroute_max_hops` was a sixth setting and went with the trace it bounded
1033	(§3.47). It stays removed: the trace is back in the process (DEVDESK-327, see
1034	[The path trace](#the-path-trace--internalnettrace)), but `nettrace.Options.MaxHops`
1035	is not wired to any setting, and the Path tab (DEVDESK-328) still traces with
1036	the engine's defaults (`nettrace.Options{}`).
1037	
1038	Two things stay hardcoded, each for a reason:
1039	
1040	- **`MinVersion: VersionTLS10`** — the handshake is *probing*, not securing.
1041	  Reporting an old version is the point; a setting could only make the tool
1042	  blind to what it exists to find.
1043	- **`InsecureSkipVerify`** — the TLS stage verifies the chain itself so it can
1044	  say *which* part failed. A setting here would collapse four checks into one
1045	  error string.
1046	
1047	`netcheck.Settings` travels **beside** `Env`, not on it: `Env` is the seam to
1048	the network, while `PingCount` and `ExpiryWarnWindow` are read by stages and
1049	never by a network call — putting a preference behind the seam would make every
1050	fake answer for one. `Settings.Normalized()` fills in anything non-positive at
1051	every entry point, so a hand-edited `0` becomes the default rather than a dial
1052	with no deadline. The view calls `checkSettings()` per run rather than capturing
1053	at construction, so a run already in flight and the config cannot disagree
1054	halfway down the pipeline.
1055	
1056	Every probe here answers from the DevDesk process. The route trace was the one
1057	exception and §3.47 removed it: `--network host` on Docker Desktop is the VM's
1058	namespace, so it traced a path from somewhere else. It is back, in the process,
1059	since DEVDESK-327 (`internal/nettrace`, below). Nothing shells out.
1060	
1061	**The `route` stage answers the question no other check can** (§3.44): when a
1062	VPN captures the default route, a host that is plainly reachable elsewhere is
1063	unreachable here, and every other row reports the *symptom* — no ICMP reply, no
1064	TCP connect — while none reports the cause. `Env.Route(ctx, ip)` returns a
1065	`RouteHop{Interface, Source, Gateway}`, and the summary names the **interface**
1066	because that is what the user recognises: "Traffic leaves through ProtonVPN"
1067	answers the question, `10.2.0.1` needs a second lookup to mean anything.
1068	
1069	`github.com/libp2p/go-netroute` is what makes it one implementation instead of
1070	three — `GetBestRoute2` on Windows, an `RTM_GETROUTE` netlink query on Linux, the
1071	routing socket on the BSDs — with no privilege anywhere and ~2 ms per lookup,
1072	measured. It depends only on `x/net` and `x/sys`, both already in the graph.
1073	
1074	Four decisions, each with a test:
1075	
1076	- **It gates nothing**, for `reach`'s reason: a machine whose routing table
1077	  cannot be read still has a perfectly answerable question about the port.
1078	- **A lookup that fails is `Unknown`, never `Fail`.** "Could not determine the
1079	  route" is not "there is no route", and rendering the first as the second is
1080	  D20. The platform error is also **localised** — Windows returns
1081	  `ERROR_NETWORK_UNREACHABLE` in the machine's own language — so it goes in a
1082	  fact and never in the summary (Rule 129).
1083	- **One family without a route is a `Warn` with its count.** That is the IPv6
1084	  case, and it is worth reporting: a client that prefers IPv6 hangs before
1085	  falling back.
1086	- **It takes its addresses from the `resolve` check's facts**, capped at
1087	  `maxRoutedAddresses`, rather than resolving again — on a round-robin name the
1088	  two could diverge and the route would describe an address no other check in the
1089	  run ever touched. `TestTheRouteStageReadsWhatTheResolveStageWrote` pins the
1090	  coupling, which is otherwise the kind that breaks in silence.
1091	
1092	## The path trace — `internal/nettrace`
1093

1551	## The socket table — `internal/ports`
1552	
1553	The machine's TCP and UDP sockets, and the process holding each, read **in this
1554	process**. `List(ctx, resolve)` and `Kill(pid)` are the whole interface.
1555	
1556	**It exists because the old one answered for the wrong machine** (D55). The
1557	Ports tab ran `ss -tupan` inside
1558	`docker run --rm --net=host --pid=host --privileged`, and on Docker Desktop
1559	`--net=host` is the namespace of the Linux VM: the tab listed the VM's NFS
1560	daemons with two-digit PIDs while not one of the host's 38 listening sockets
1561	appeared, and `K` sent SIGKILL to a process of the VM under the impression it was
1562	freeing a port on the machine. The sentence explaining this has sat at the top of
1563	`docker.runDiagHost` since §3.33 rapatriated DNS, ICMP, TCP, TLS and HTTP for
1564	exactly the same reason; `RunSS` and `KillProcess` were the two nobody pulled it
1565	for. **Under Linux the defect did not exist**, which is why it went unnoticed:
1566	the tab was right on the platform it was written on.
1567	
1568	No new dependency: `gopsutil/v4/net` was already imported by
1569	`internal/metrics/host.go`. Windows reads iphlpapi, Linux `/proc`, macOS and the
1570	BSDs `lsof` — the last is a subprocess, but one the system supplies, and it
1571	replaces a privileged container.
1572	
1573	Four decisions, each with a test:
1574	
1575	- **The process names come from one enumeration, not one call per socket.** The
1576	  obvious `process.NewProcess(pid).Name()` goes through `OpenProcess` on
1577	  Windows and needs rights over the target: measured here, **98 of 189** sockets
1578	  came back *Access denied*, so the Process column would have been empty for
1579	  every service on the box. `Processes()` reads a Toolhelp32 snapshot instead
1580	  and named **294 of 294** in 11 ms, elevated or not. The bulk call is not an
1581	  optimisation over the per-PID one — it is the difference between a column that
1582	  is filled in and one that is not.
1583	- **A PID of zero carries no PID.** It is the system declining to attribute the
1584	  socket, and `K` keys on that field: left as `"0"` the row would look killable,
1585	  and process 0 is a whole process group on Unix. `Kill` refuses it a second
1586	  time, on the model of §3.23's double guard. The name is a *separate* question:
1587	  a row may know which process holds the socket and not what it is called, and
1588	  it must stay killable — that is the row the user is acting on.
1589	- **Two states are normalised, and neither is cosmetic.** An unconnected
1590	  datagram socket is `NONE` on Linux and nothing at all on Windows, so the same
1591	  socket read differently depending on where DevDesk ran — and the `l`/`e`
1592	  filters with it. `ESTABLISHED` is shortened to `ESTAB` because the State
1593	  column is ten cells wide, so the long spelling renders as `ESTABLISHE`.
1594	- **`n` resolves the host half only.** `ss` without `-n` also turned 22 into
1595	  `ssh`; Go resolves a name to a port and not the other way round, so honouring
1596	  that would mean shipping a copy of `/etc/services` and calling the result the
1597	  system's answer. Saying less beats saying something the system did not.
1598	
1599	The reverse-DNS cache is **package-level**, because the lookups run inside a
1600	`Cmd` and a `Cmd` may not touch the model (Rule 110). It caches the failures
1601	too: a machine talking to hosts with no PTR record would otherwise re-ask for
1602	every one of them on every two-second tick — the storm the cache exists to
1603	prevent, arriving through the failures instead of the successes. Wildcard,
1604	loopback and unspecified addresses are never asked at all.
1605	
1606	**`Kill` signals with the rights DevDesk has**, which is the visible change:
1607	another user's process, or a service, now comes back refused by the operating
1608	system instead of succeeding against the wrong machine.
1609	
1610	**So the refusal has to be legible, and `K` has to say when it cannot even
1611	try** (§3.49). Two different questions, and only one of them is answerable
1612	before the keypress:
1613	
1614	- **No PID, no key.** A socket the system declines to attribute carries an empty
1615	  `PID`, and `K` is greyed on that row (Rule 130) — it used to be advertised
1616	  everywhere and warn only once pressed.
1617	- **Whether the OS will accept the signal is the attempt's answer**, never the
1618	  header's, so a row with a PID stays lit even when the kill is certain to be
1619	  refused. `killFailureMessage` classifies the failure with `errors.Is` through
1620	  the `%w` wrapping `Kill` applies: `os.ErrPermission` reads *Refused by the
1621	  system*, `os.ErrProcessDone` reads *no longer running*, anything else keeps
1622	  the generic line. `Failed to kill PID N` made those the same sentence.
1623	
1624	The platform error never reaches the screen — measured, PID 4 on this machine
1625	answers `OpenProcess: Accès refusé.`, in the machine's own language, which is
1626	the route stage's rule (§3.44). Also measured, and written down rather than
1627	discovered: **the "already gone" branch does not fire on Windows**, where a
1628	nonexistent PID fails `OpenProcess` with `ERROR_INVALID_PARAMETER` and maps to
1629	neither sentinel. Mapping that code would be a guess, and the row disappears on
1630	the next two-second refresh anyway.
1631	
1632	**Nothing in the application runs `--network host` any more** (§3.47). §3.33
1633	brought DNS, ICMP, TCP, TLS and HTTP into the process, §3.43 the socket table,
1634	§3.44 the interfaces, and §3.47 removed the route trace — the last one. That is
1635	the checkable form of "DevDesk never claims to answer for a machine that is not
1636	yours", and it closes **D57**.
1637	
1638	**The route trace was deleted rather than rewritten** (it came back in the
1639	process with DEVDESK-327, see [The path trace](#the-path-trace--internalnettrace);
1640	what follows is the history of §3.47), and the reasons are worth
1641	keeping because they are the shape of the decision, not of this feature:
1642	
1643	- it answered for the **wrong machine** — `--network host` traced from the Docker
1644	  Desktop VM, so the hops were the VM's;
1645	- what people came for has a **better answer**: `netcheck`'s Local route check
1646	  names the interface and source address from *this* machine, in 2 ms, which is
1647	  the split-tunnel question;
1648	- rewriting it was **three unmeasured unknowns** — reading ICMP `TIME_EXCEEDED`
1649	  without a raw socket on three platforms, a per-packet TTL `pro-bing` does not
1650	  expose, and a TCP mode needing the ICMP error of an outgoing connection.
1651	
1652	`H` went back into `keymap.Free()` beside `J`, `Q` and `Z`: a letter an action
1653	has just released is redeclared free, or it stays reserved for something that no
1654	longer exists.
1655	
1656	The OCI connectivity test — the last container DevDesk started from a
1657	network-inspect overlay, and with it `network.connectivity_image` and its
1658	three-link migration chain (`docker.network_tool_image` →
1659	`network.tool_image` → `network.connectivity_image`) — has been removed. The
1660	network-inspect overlay itself (`:oci` → Networks → `enter`) stays; only the
1661	`c` key it used to offer, and everything behind it, is gone.
1662	
1663	## The port forwarder — `internal/forward`
1664	
1665	A local TCP port redirected to a `host:port`, **in this process** and with no
1666	privilege: a `net.Listen` and two `io.Copy`. `Registry.Open(port, target)`,
1667	`Toggle(id)`, `Close(id)`, `CloseAll()`, `List()`, `Restore(entries)` and
1668	`Entries()` are the whole interface; the messages a view exchanges with the router live in the same package so a view
1669	never imports `internal/app`.
1670	
1671	**The router owns the registry** (`shared.State.Forwards`, built once in
1672	`newWithSize`). `reinitializeViews` drops every view on a config save and on a
1673	context switch, so a listener held by the Forward tab would stay bound with
1674	nothing left to close it. The tab asks (`forward.Open` / `Close` / `Refresh`) and
1675	is told (`forward.ChangedMsg`, broadcast to every held view, on screen or not).
1676	Forwards **survive a context switch** — one belongs to no context.
1677	
1678	### Persistence (§3.75)
1679	
1680	The **listener** cannot outlive the process, but the **intent** can: every
1681	forward is written to `~/.devdesk/forwards.yaml` and reopened at the next launch.
1682	It is a file of its own rather than a key of `config.yaml`, because the config
1683	is per context and is reloaded on every switch, and a forward belongs to no
1684	context.
1685	
1686	| Piece | Where | Does |
1687	|---|---|---|
1688	| `Store` (`store.go`) | `internal/forward` | `Load` / `Save` the `[]Entry` (`local_port`, `target`, `paused`), `version: 1` |
1689	| `Registry.Entries()` | `internal/forward` | describes what is *wanted*, in creation order, live or not |
1690	| `Registry.Restore()` | `internal/forward` | reopens the entries at startup, binds in parallel |
